pavilion_steward.text: Hush, there is a rehearsal. Oh, it has not started. Hello then!
The Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod brings in choirs and dancers from all over the world every July.
It began in 1947, two years after the war ended, and the first competitors came from more than a dozen countries.
The Pavilion holds thousands. When they all sing, you can feel it in your teeth.

then.text: The Chair's back, level as a snooker table. Emrys has been in twice to check it. He sits on it very gently.
The Eisteddfod has run in Llangollen since 1947, and the town sings through it. Thank you for letting us keep the chair, and the peace.
The plinth, the towpath, the tearooms, the chapel, the terrace and the bench. That's every lead. Who took it?

else.text: Still gathering? Good. A rushed accusation in Llangollen ends with someone being hurt, and then the choir takes sides.

The Chair has never sat true, you know. Back left leg a hair short, ever since it was made. Emrys Bowen carved it in 1998, and he apologises every July.
He'd never take it, mind. Too shy. I'm only saying it rocks.
Have a look at the plinth first. Right there, on the dais. Go on, I'll not touch it.
Eirlys Mathias, Eisteddfod secretary, keeper of the schedule, the keys and the biscuit tin.

The Eisteddfod Chair has vanished from its plinth overnight. A carved oak chair, awarded at the closing concert. Not the bardic Chair of the National Eisteddfod, which is another thing entirely and another town every August, but ours, and it matters.

Three people have been muttering: a rival conductor, a caterer, and, well, I'd rather not say. Look, ask, write it down. Your Fieldbook has a Casebook tab; press Run on the Fieldbook until you find it.
When you're sure, come back and name them. A wrong name will cost you standing, and rightly.
Case opened: The Stolen Eisteddfod Chair.
